sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.content: The exploration of intelligence and the feasibility of machines with cognitive abilities is a compelling pursuit in the scientific community. In the Artificial Intelligence (AI) domain, researchersarediligentlystrivingtoadvancemethodologiesfordevelopingintelligentmachines. OneofthelatestadvancementsisLargeLanguageModels(LLMs),whichhavebecomepopular in both academia and industry. These LLMs are impressively effective and can achieve almost human-like performance in certain tasks [274]. Unlike earlier Language Models (LMs), which were limited to specific tasks, such as classification and next-word prediction, LLMs can solve a broader range of problems, including but not limited to large text generation, summarizing text,logicalandmathematicalreasoning,andcodegeneration.Inaddition,withefficientprompt engineering [222], LLMs can adapt to different contexts and/or even accomplish new tasks without further training or fine-tuning. However, these highly efficient LLMs are not flawless. The vulnerabilities of these LLMs have not been extensively explored on a large scale from a security and privacy perspective. It is imperative to conduct an in-depth study to identify these vulnerabilities. This article comprehensively illustrates the security and privacy challenges in LLMs,alongwithdefensemechanismsandfutureresearchopportunities. Motivation. LLMs require a huge amount of data from the Internet in addition to meticulously annotated textual data for training/fine-tuning to enhance the model’s predictive performance. In contrast to carefully created annotated data, the freely available texts on the Internet may exhibit poor data quality and unintended leakages of private personal information [107]. For instance, casual interactions with these models may accidentally leak Personally Identifiable Information (PII), as highlighted in the work of Carlini et al. [20], which may violate existing privacy laws, such as the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996 (HIPAA) [30], the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) [208], and the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA) [14]. Following the launch of ChatGPT [149] and GPT-4 [3], numerous researchinitiativeshavefocusedonassessingthemacrossvariousdimensions.Theseevaluations considered various aspects of Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks, such as correctness, robustness,rationality,reliability,and,notably,theidentificationandevaluationofvulnerabilities relatedtoprivacyrisksandsecurityissues.AssessmentofaLLM’sprivacyrisksandsecurityhas paramountimportanceforseveralreasons.First,itwillcontributetoanin-depthunderstanding of the strengths and weaknesses of LLMs. Second, a comprehensive evaluation of security and privacy vulnerabilities in LLMs will potentially inspire efforts and advances toward secure and privacy-preserving human-LLM interactions. Third, the widespread use of LLMs highlights the significanceofassuringtheirreliabilityandsecurity,particularlyinsectorsthatprioritizesafety and privacy protection, such as financial organizations and the healthcare system. Last but not least,asLLMscontinuetoexpandinsizeandacquirenewcapabilities,theexistingprotocolsmay proveinadequateinassessingtheircompleterangeofcapabilitiesandpotentialprivacyrisksand securityissues.Ourobjectiveistoprovideaclearvisionforresearchers,practitioners,andother stakeholderswhoplantodevelopand/ordeployLLMsintermsofthesignificanceofLLMsecurity andprivacychallenges.Thisinvolvesreviewingexistingstudiesinthebroadareaofsecurity,pri- vacy,andtheirintersections,andnotablyhighlightingfutureresearchdirectionstodesignnovel evaluationprotocolsandattackmethods,aswellasdefensemechanismstailoredtotheevolving LLMlandscape. Prompt hacking manipulates the input prompts of the LLM to obtain the desired output by a malicious user. With proper malicious prompts, even a well-trained model can produce misleading or malicious content [140]. The two types of goal-based prompt hacking strategies are described next. 4.1.1 PromptInjection. PromptinjectionentailsbypassingLLMsafetyfiltersbymanipulating the model with meticulously crafted prompts that cause the model to disregard the original prompt. It may cause unintended consequences, such as data leakage, unauthorized access, and hate speech generation [173]. Recent studies explored several prompt injection attacks in LLMs. A straightforward way to mislead an LLM is to instruct it to ignore the previous prompt. This methodisacombinationofgoalhijacking andpromptleaking [156].Goalhijacking(alsoknown as “Prompt Divergence” [180]) is defined as the manipulation of the original prompt goal to mislead the model to generate a specific target phrase. In prompt leaking, the original prompt goal is redirected to the objective of reproducing the partial or entire original prompt. sections.content: ProtectingLLMsfromsecurityandprivacyattacksisimperativetopreservetheirreliabilityand integrity [148]. Here, we review existing studies to mitigate the LLM vulnerabilities and defend againstemergingsecurityandprivacythreats. ACMComput.Surv.,Vol.57,No.6,Article152.Publicationdate:February2025. SecurityandPrivacyChallengesofLargeLanguageModels:ASurvey 152:17 6.1 DefenseagainstSecurityAttacksonLLMs DefenseagainstPromptInjection.Limitedstudiesexploredthedefensestrategyagainstprompt injection attacks in LLMs. A prevention/detection-based defense technique has been reported to systematically present existing defense mechanisms against prompt injection attacks [121]. Prevention-based defenses, as outlined in the work of Jain et al. [88], are designed to thwart the successful execution of tasks injected into an LLM-integrated application. These preventive measuresinvolvepre-processingthedataprompttoeliminatetheinjectedtask’sinstruction/data and/orredesigningtheinstructionpromptitself.Tothwartadversarialprompts,thereareseveral techniques, such as paraphrasing [88], re-tokenization [88], data prompt isolation, and instruc- tional prevention [171]. Paraphrasing disrupts the sequence of injected data, such as injected instructionsandspecialcharacterinsertion.Re-tokenizationaimstobreakthesequenceofinjected instructions, task-ignoring text, special characters, and fake responses within a compromised dataprompt.Thisdisruptiondiminishestheefficacyofpromptinjectionattacks.Detection-based defensesarefocusedondeterminingtheintegrityofagivendataprompt[88,190,215].Notably, the proactive detection method [175] has proven effective in identifying instances of prompt injection attacks. Perplexity-based detection is a kind of prompt-based detection. The idea is to addinformationorinstructionstoadataprompt,whichdegradesitsqualityandleadstoincreased perplexity.Consequently,adatapromptisconsideredtobecompromisedifitsperplexityexceeds a specified threshold [66]. Since an LLM-integrated application is tailored for a specific task, grantingitpriorknowledgeoftheanticipatedresponse,detectingacompromiseddatapromptis feasiblewhenthegeneratedresponsedeviatesfromtheproperanswerforthedesiredtask[175]. For example, if the desired task is spam detection and the response does not align with “spam” or “non-spam,” they imply a compromise. Notably, this defense is ineffective when the injected task and desired task share the same type (e.g., both being related to spam detection). Effective protectionstrategiesagainstP2SQLinjectionattacksareavailableandmaybeincorporatedinto the LangChain framework as extensions [155]. For example, since P2SQL injection attacks can manipulate chatbots by arbitrarily executing different queries [155], controlling database roles andpermissionstolimittheexecutionofundesiredSQLstatementswhenaccessingtableswith sensitiveinformationcanbeaviabletechniquetodefendsuchattacks.Conversely,indirectattacks involvemaliciousinputresidinginthedatabase,enablinginterferencewithLLM-generatedSQL queriesandpotentiallyunderminingtheeffectivenessofthesedefenses.Liuetal.[123]performed anempiricalstudytocomprehensivelyformalizeandbenchmarkseveralpromptinjectionattacks and defenses. They found that the prevalent prevention-based and detection-based defense techniques are insufficient to mitigate the risks of advanced optimization-based attacks (e.g., JudgeDeceiver[185]). As a built-in safety mechanism, pre-processing-based techniques, detecting and blocking the inputsoroutputs,andsemanticcontentfilteringhavebeenemployedtopreventgeneratingunde- siredorinappropriatecontentsfromLLMsthroughjailbreakingattacks,whichcouldeffectively mitigatepotentialharm[131].Kumaretal.[103]proposedanapproachtoapplyasafetyfilteron thesubstringsofinputprompts,whichprovidescertifiablerobustnessguarantees.Thedrawback ofthisapproachliesinthemethod’scomplexity,whichincreasesproportionallywithinputprompt length.Wuetal.[229]proposeasystem-modeself-remindertodefendagainstjailbreakingattacks underpretendingorrole-playingscenarios,whichcandrasticallyreducethejailbreakingsuccess rate from 67.21% to 19.34%. One potential simple defense strategy is to identify the presence of “red-flagged” keywords [221], which strictly violates the usage policies of the LLM vendors, such as OpenAI [44]. Recently, Zhang et al. [262] proposed a goal prioritization technique that prioritizesgeneratingharmlessresponsesoverhelpfulonesattheinferencephase.Thistechnique cansignificantlyreducethesuccessrateofjailbreakingattacksinChatGPTandLlama2.However, ACMComput.Surv.,Vol.57,No.6,Article152.Publicationdate:February2025. 152:18 B.C.Dasetal. these basic defense mechanisms may not be sufficient to prevent jailbreaking attacks with care- fully crafted tricky prompts, such as privilege escalation. Furthermore, preventing these attacks stillposesasignificantchallengebecausetheeffectivedefensesmayimpactmodelutility[110].By far,SmoothLLMisaneffectivedefensestrategyagainstexistingjailbreakingattacksproposedby Zouetal.[276].Itcanbeappliedformitigatingtheinstruction-basedattacks,suchasAutoDAN [118],DAN[183],andPAIR[23].Itinvolvesatwo-stepprocess.First,copiesofaspecifiedinput promptareduplicatedandperturbed.Subsequently,theoutputsproducedforeachperturbedcopy areaggregated.Thedesiderataencompassfourkeyproperties:attackmitigation(reducesattack success rate 100% and 50% for Llama 2 and Vicuna, respectively), non-conservatism, efficiency (in terms of computational resources), and compatibility (different LLMs). For preventing the advanced attack methods, such as MSJ [108] and MasterKey [44], an unsafe prompt detection andfilteringtechniquemayeffectivelyrefusetoprovidetheinappropriateresponseintendedby the adversary. MDP [235] faces challenges in various NLP tasks, such as paraphrasing and sentence similarity [62]. Its performance under few-shot learning remains uncertain due to a lack of practical evaluation. While MDP has shown strength against earlier backdoor attacks, it may not be effective against more recent attacks, such as BadPrompt [18] andBToP[239].Perplexity-basedmethodsandfiltering-basedmethodsmaynotworkwellwhen attackersusesynonymoustriggerkeys[80].Furthermore,developingdynamicdefensemethods thatconsidertheprecedingfactorsisachallengingtaskforthefuture.Currently,thepredominant focusofinvestigationonbackdoorattacksrevolvesaroundtextclassificationinLLMs.However, a significant gap exists in the literature concerning investigations into mitigation to backdoor attacksonvarioustasksforwhichLLMsfindwidespreadapplication,suchastextsummarization andtextgeneration[244].Forpoisoningattacks,thereisnotyeteffectivemitigationforProAttack [264] and BadPrompt [18]. Defense techniques, such as dataset cleaning and removing near duplicate poisoned samples and anomalies, may slow down the model development process to defend against data poisoning attacks. Other defense methods, such as stopping training after certain epochs, achieve a moderate defense against poisoning attacks but degrade the model utility [210]. Gradient perturbation [78] and DP-SGD-based methods [1] are frequently used to defendagainstprivacyattacksinLLMs.However,arecentstudyhasdemonstratedthataddinga standardlevelofrandomnoiseintothegradientupdatemightnotalwaysworkwelltoprevent gradient leakage attacks on medical images [42]. An open language model (OLMo) has been introducedtoprovideaccesstothedata,code,andmodel[191]tofacilitateopenresearchonLMs. While adhering to established practices for obscuring PII exposure and removing toxic content, theapproachlacksexplicitdiscussionofattackimpactsandriskmitigationexploredinthissurvey. Futureresearchcouldleveragesecuremulti-partycomputation[39]tocounterprivacyattacks. FutureresearchinitiativesforenhancingsecurityandprivacyinLLMscanbedirectedtoward several key areas. An ideal defense method should be able to effectively achieve a balance betweenmodelutilityandsecurityandprivacyprotection.Thedevelopmentofreal-timeprivacy monitoring systems is essential to improve the resilience of privacy-preserving LLMs. This necessitates the exploration of robust detection techniques against various security and privacy attacks. Furthermore, a thorough evaluation of less-explored defense techniques, such as secure multi-party computation, is necessary to assess their effectiveness against LLM vulnerabilities. Finally,leveragingthecapabilitiesofXAIcanimprovetransparencyinLLMdefensemechanisms. RoleofXAIinEnhancingSecurityandPrivacyofLLMs.TheLLM’sabilitytomakedecisions on various learning tasks is often criticized due to its black-box nature (e.g., non-interpretable weights).Itmakesitmorechallengingforthenewpractitionersanddevelopersofthisfield,asit hinderstheirabilitytoclearlyinterpretandunderstanditsapplication,particularlyincriticalcases. XAI can help to bridge this gap by developing methods to interpret and explain complex LLM systems,thedecision-makingprocess,andoutputs[19].Conductingstudiesandresearchtobuild explainablemethodsishighlyessentialtomaketheusageofLLMsmorereliableandtrustworthy. XAIcanprovidetransparentinsightsintotheinferenceprocessandthedynamicweightassign- ment by the attention mechanism of the LLMs, which enhances interpretability by highlighting themostinfluentialinputfeaturesthatcontributetoitspredictions.Thisexplainabilitymakesthe modelmoretrustworthyandensuresthatitsoutputisexplainable.XAIhasshownitspotentialin several real-world AI applications, such as cybersecurity [169] and enhancing data privacy [53]. InML,severaltechniquesexist,suchasLIME(LocalInterpretableModel-agnosticExplanations) [167]andSHAP(SHapleyAdditiveexPlanations)[126],whichofferinsightsintomodelbehavior ACMComput.Surv.,Vol.57,No.6,Article152.Publicationdate:February2025. The explainability of code generation models, suchasCodeBERT[56]andGraphCodeBERT[69],wasproposedtounderstandcodesyntaxand semantics[246].Inaddition,thead-hocexplanationfurtherclarifiesthemodel’sdecision[116]. TheroleofXAIinthesecurityandprivacyaspectofLLMiscrucial.Specificallyinitsdevelop- ment phase, having prior knowledge about the attackers’ ability (e.g., model’s black-box access, injecting poisonous instances to the training/fine-tuning data) and the vulnerable components (training/fine-tuning data and the model itself) of LLM systems will assist in developing robust techniquesagainstsecurityandprivacyattacks.However,XAImayexposecriticalaspectsofthe LLMs,includingtheirarchitecture,components,andthedynamicweightallocationbytheatten- tion mechanism that contribute to predictions. For example, revealing the white-box nature of the model may facilitate the attacker’s access to the model, increasing the risk of gradient leak- ageattacksorMIA[53].Linetal.[115]proposedanXAIapproachthatcanidentifythetriggers (backdoorattack)thatmisleadthemodeltocontributetoclassificationerrors.AnXAItechniqueis developedbyLietal.[115]toidentifyandquantifytheinfluenceofrawdatafeaturesonsuccess- fulMIAs.Thisapproachidentifiestheinfluentialneuronscontributingtocompromisingprivate dataandsubsequentlytrainsanMIAensemblemodelusingattackfeaturesderivedfromthese- lected neurons [115]. XAI techniques in image models (e.g., Grad-CAM [174]) may compromise model privacy under various attacks, such as gradient leakage attacks and MIA. In some cases, XAIenablesmoreaccuratereconstructionofprivatetrainingdatacomparedtomodelsthatrely solelyonpredictions[266].XAI-awaremodelextractionattack(XaMEA)wasproposedtoexploit spatialknowledgefromdecisionexplanations[241].Itillustratedthatthetransparencyprovided by XAI may facilitate the attacker’s access to the model, making it easier to exploit it. This in- creasedexplainabilitycanmakethemodelmorevulnerabletomodelextractionattackscompared topredictiononlymodels.However,thevulnerabilitiesmentionedpreviouslyaremostlyexplored forDNNs.InLLMs,thevulnerabilitiesintheXAIcontexthavebeenexploredtoalimitedextent. Moreover,severaluniquecharacteristicsofLLMsaredifferentfromDNNs,suchaslarge-scaledata andmodelparameters,task-agnostic,andsemanticlanguageunderstanding,whichmakeitmore challengingtodesignXAImethodsforbetterinterpretations.Thecomprehensiveinterpretation ofLLMvulnerabilitiesunderXAI,includingbackdoorattacks,MIAs,andmodelextractionattacks, hasyettobefullyexplored.Additionally,vulnerabilitiesrelatedtopromptinjectionandjailbreak- ing attacks in the context of XAI still remain unexplored. However, thisenhancedaccessibilitycanmakethemmorevulnerabletoattackswhenXAItechniquesare employed.Thus,theseLLMsmaybemoresusceptibletoattacksduetoXAI.Furtherresearchises- sentialtofullyunderstandtheextentandimpactofattackers’capabilitiesunderXAI.Additionally, mitigationtechniquesshouldbedevelopedinaccordancewiththeidentifiedrisksandimpacts.

sections.heading: 9 Conclusion
sections.content: LLMs lend themselves as strong tools for comprehending complex linguistic patterns and gen- erating logical and contextually coherent responses. However, such powerful models also entail potentialsecurityandprivacyrisks.Inthissurvey,wefirstprovidedadetailedoverviewofLLMs’ security and privacy challenges. We then discussed and analyzed the LLM vulnerabilities from bothsecurityandprivacyaspects,existingmitigationanddefensestrategiesagainstthesesecurity attacksandprivacyattacks,aswellashighlightedtheirstrengthsandlimitations.Inourinvestiga- tion,wefoundthatLLMsarehighlyvulnerabletothediscussedattacks.Theexistingmitigation techniquesthatareapplicabletorelativelysmallLMscouldpotentiallybeusedforLLMs.However, extensiveresearchisneededtoevaluateandtailortheexistingsolutionstoLLMs.Basedonour analysis,weoutlinedfutureresearchdirectionsfocusingonsecurityandprivacyaspects,pointed ACMComput.Surv.,Vol.57,No.6,Article152.Publicationdate:February2025. 152:28 B.C.Dasetal. outkeyresearchgaps,andillustratedopenresearchproblems.Theoverarchinggoalistoenhance the reliability and utility of LLMs by comprehensively exploring and addressing these vulnera- bilitieswhileprovidingpathwaysforfutureresearchtowardsecureandprivacy-preservingLLM systems. Security and Privacy Challenges of Large Language Models:
A Survey
BADHAN CHANDRA DAS, KnightFoundationSchoolofComputingandInformationSciences(KFS-
CIS),FloridaInternationalUniversity,Miami,UnitedStates
M. HADI AMINI, KnightFoundationSchoolofComputingandInformationSciences(KFSCIS),Florida
InternationalUniversity,Miami,UnitedStates
YANZHAO WU, Knight Foundation School of Computing and Information Sciences (KFSCIS), Florida
InternationalUniversity,Miami,UnitedStates
Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated extraordinary capabilities and contributed to multiple
fields,suchasgeneratingandsummarizingtext,languagetranslation,andquestion-answering.Today,LLMs
havebecomequitepopulartoolsinnaturallanguageprocessingtasks,withthecapabilitytoanalyzecompli-
catedlinguisticpatternsandproviderelevantresponsesdependingonthecontext.Whileofferingsignificant
advantages,thesemodelsarealsovulnerabletosecurityandprivacyattacks,suchasjailbreakingattacks,data
poisoningattacks,andpersonallyidentifiableinformationleakageattacks.Thissurveyprovidesathorough
review of the security and privacy challenges of LLMs, along with the application-based risks in various
domains, such as transportation, education, and healthcare. We assess the extent of LLM vulnerabilities,
investigateemergingsecurityandprivacyattacksagainstLLMs,andreviewpotentialdefensemechanisms.
Additionally,thesurveyoutlinesexistingresearchgapsandhighlightsfutureresearchdirections.

1 Introduction
The exploration of intelligence and the feasibility of machines with cognitive abilities is a
compelling pursuit in the scientific community. In the Artificial Intelligence (AI) domain,
researchersarediligentlystrivingtoadvancemethodologiesfordevelopingintelligentmachines.
OneofthelatestadvancementsisLargeLanguageModels(LLMs),whichhavebecomepopular
in both academia and industry. These LLMs are impressively effective and can achieve almost
human-like performance in certain tasks [274]. Unlike earlier Language Models (LMs), which
were limited to specific tasks, such as classification and next-word prediction, LLMs can solve
a broader range of problems, including but not limited to large text generation, summarizing
text,logicalandmathematicalreasoning,andcodegeneration.Inaddition,withefficientprompt
engineering [222], LLMs can adapt to different contexts and/or even accomplish new tasks
without further training or fine-tuning. However, these highly efficient LLMs are not flawless.
The vulnerabilities of these LLMs have not been extensively explored on a large scale from a
security and privacy perspective. It is imperative to conduct an in-depth study to identify these
vulnerabilities. This article comprehensively illustrates the security and privacy challenges in
LLMs,alongwithdefensemechanismsandfutureresearchopportunities.
Motivation. LLMs require a huge amount of data from the Internet in addition to meticulously
annotated textual data for training/fine-tuning to enhance the model’s predictive performance.

4.1 PromptHacking
As LLMs work with interaction-based question and answering systems with their users, they
need to put specific queries to the prompt, then it generates outputs based on training. Prompt
hacking manipulates the input prompts of the LLM to obtain the desired output by a malicious
user. With proper malicious prompts, even a well-trained model can produce misleading or
malicious content [140]. The two types of goal-based prompt hacking strategies are described
next.
4.1.1 PromptInjection. PromptinjectionentailsbypassingLLMsafetyfiltersbymanipulating
the model with meticulously crafted prompts that cause the model to disregard the original
prompt. It may cause unintended consequences, such as data leakage, unauthorized access, and
hate speech generation [173]. Recent studies explored several prompt injection attacks in LLMs.
A straightforward way to mislead an LLM is to instruct it to ignore the previous prompt. This
methodisacombinationofgoalhijacking andpromptleaking [156].Goalhijacking(alsoknown
as “Prompt Divergence” [180]) is defined as the manipulation of the original prompt goal to
mislead the model to generate a specific target phrase. In prompt leaking, the original prompt
goal is redirected to the objective of reproducing the partial or entire original prompt. Perez
andRibeiro[156]performedanearlystudyonpromptinjectionattacks,considering35different
application scenarios built on OpenAI models. Their research explored two primary attack
